translations.text: To the Jewish brothers who are in the regions of Egypt, from the Jewish brothers in Jerusalem and the brothers in Judea: greetings, with abundant peace.
May God be generous to you and remember the covenant he made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, his faithful servants.
May he give you a heart to worship him in everything and to do his will with devoted souls and willing hearts.
May he open the eyes and ears of your hearts to his law and commandments, and grant peace.
May he hear your petitions, be gracious to you, and not abandon you in times of distress.
And now we are already praying for you. In the years of the reign of Demetrius,
In the one hundred and sixty-ninth year, we Jews wrote this to you during the distress that had come upon us, at the time when Jason and those with him turned away from the holy land and the kingdom.

they set fire to the gate and shed innocent blood. We offered prayers to the Lord, and he heard us. We presented vows, incense, and sacrifices with fine flour, and we set out the bread of the Presence.
And now you should observe the days of the Feast of Tabernacles in the month of Chislev.

In the eighty-eighth year. From the people of Jerusalem, the council of the people of Judea, and Judas, to Aristobulus, the teacher of King Ptolemy, who is himself of the family of the anointed priests, [?] the Jews in the regions of Egypt: greetings and peace to you.
Having been delivered by God from great afflictions, we give him great thanks, for when we were prepared for battle in a war against the king, he himself threw into turmoil and scattered those
who had come and surrounded the holy city, keeping it under siege. For at the time when the ruler himself went into the regions of Persia,
With countless, innumerable troops, they fell and were destroyed there around the temple of Ananaea [?]. In their foolish deliberations, they plotted concerning the temple of Nehemiah.
For Antiochus himself and the friends with him had arrived and taken up residence there, intending to take all the treasures under the pretext of paying the mercenaries.

the priests of the temple set everything before him. He agreed to enter with a few men. When he had entered the halls, they boldly closed the outer gates of the walls through which Antiochus had entered.

They opened the hidden windows beneath the ceiling supports and began pouring down huge [?] through them. There they killed the leader together with his company. After tearing them to pieces inside, they brought out their heads and threw them from the wall into the midst of the soldiers.
For all this, blessed is God, who delivered the ungodly into our hands.

Now, since we intended to purify the temple on the twenty-fifth day of the month of Chislev, we thought it good to inform you of this too, so that you also might observe it according to the ordinances of the feasts of Tabernacles and of the fire, as when Nehemiah built the temple and the altar on which he offered burnt offerings.

For at the time when our fathers were taken away to the regions of Persia, the priests who were devoted to their service in those days secretly took fire from the altar and carried it away. They hid it in recesses at the sides of dry wells. There they carefully [?] concealed the place, so that the entire place would be out of sight.

After many years had passed, when it was God's will, Nehemiah, by order of the king of Persia, sent the descendants of those high priests who had concealed and hidden the fire to bring it back. When they returned, they reported, saying, “We found no fire there, but we found thick, sluggish water.”
Then he ordered them to go, draw it out with a pump, and bring it. When the time came for the burnt offerings, Nehemiah the high priest ordered them to sprinkle it over the wood and the sacrifices.

When they had done this, a little time passed, and the sun cast its light through the clouds upon it. A flame blazed over the wood on the altar and consumed the burnt offerings, so that everyone was amazed.
The priests raised their voices and began to give praise while the burnt offerings were being consumed. Jonathan led, speaking on behalf of Nehemiah, and the others joined in after him.
This was the form of the prayer: “Lord, Lord, God of all creation, awesome, mighty, true, righteous, and merciful, you alone are the gracious King.”
You alone provide everything for everyone. You alone are just and true, the eternal Almighty, who saves Israel from every evil, who made the fathers chosen in this way and sanctified them.
Accept this sacrifice on behalf of all your people, and preserve your inheritance.
Sanctify and gather those of us scattered in captivity. Free those who are enslaved to dishonorable and unclean people. Look upon your servants, so that the nations may know that you are our God.
Strike with your blows those who oppressed us, the unclean and dishonorable nations who are now proud and arrogant toward us.
And plant your people in your holy place, as Moses said.
And the priests pronounced their blessings.
And the burnt offerings gradually burned, blazed up, and were consumed. When the sacrifices were finished, Nehemiah ordered the remaining water to be poured over the rocks.
When this happened, the fire flared up still more over it. As the flames shone, the altar once again caught fire and blazed up, and whatever remained was also consumed.

When these events became publicly known and word reached the king, people came and saw the place where the captive priests had hidden the fire. Water had gushed out from there, and the priests who were with Nehemiah had completed and sanctified their burnt offerings.
Then, when the king had established the truth of these events, he ordered the place to be enclosed on all sides, and they built a temple.
The king gave a gift from there to anyone he wished to favor, and those to whom he gave brought him many possessions.
Those who were with Nehemiah named it Nephthae, which in translation means “purifier.” But many called it Euphratha.

This is found written in the earlier books: the prophet Jeremiah afterward ordered them to take some of that fire, as is indicated; and the prophet gave instructions to their descendants who came after them.

He laid down rules for them, so that they would not forget the commands of the Lord or go astray in their thoughts when they saw carved idols, fashioned images of gold and silver, and whatever ornaments were on them.
With these instructions he urged them not to forget the law in their hearts.

And it was written in those books as follows: according to the heavenly command, the prophet ordered them to take along the tent of worship and the ark of the covenant, as Moses went up to that mountain to see God’s inheritance.

Then the prophet Jeremiah reached that place and found secure caves amid thick woods. He brought the tent of worship, the ark of the covenant, and the altar of incense there, placed them inside, and closed up the entrances himself.
Those who were with him then went to mark the place, but they could not find any path to it at all.

When Jeremiah learned this, he began to rebuke them and said, “How do you not know that the command is to keep this place unknown until the Lord of lords is pleased with his creatures and God commands the assembly of his people to be gathered?”

“Then the Lord will reveal these things, and the glory of the Lord will appear in a pillar of cloud, as in the time of Moses, and as Solomon prayed that the place might be greatly sanctified for the Lord.”
He made it clear in this way that, with wise counsel, they offered the sacrifices for the dedication and completion of the temple.

Just as Moses stood in prayer before the Lord, and fire came down from heaven and consumed the wood and the burnt offerings of the sacrifices, so Solomon also stood in prayer, and fire came down and consumed the burnt offerings on the altar.
For Moses had not been commanded to make the sin offerings available to eat; the fire would come down and consume the sacrifices.
Likewise, Solomon carried this out for the full eight days.

They searched the ancient books, the records of inquiries made in the days of Nehemiah, who gathered all these together as his own, along with other books of the kings and prophets, all of David’s writings, and other royal decrees issued on various matters in honor of the temple. He amassed them all in one place.
Likewise, Judas gathered into one place everything that had been ruined and scattered by the wars, and it is now preserved intact among us.
And now, if you have need of them in any way, send to us, and we will have them brought to you.
You will do a good thing if you observe the festival days regularly.
But God himself, who saved all his people and restored them all to their inheritance—the kingdom, the priesthood, and holiness—
as he also promised through the covenants, will, we hope in the Lord, very soon gather them into the holy place.
For he has indeed saved us from great evils and restored the place to holiness.
Now concerning Judas Maccabeus and his brothers, the purification of the great temple, and the dedication of the altar,
and concerning the battles against Antiochus Epiphanes or against his son Eupator,

or the appearances from heaven on behalf of those who courageously upheld the laws, or who took courage to heart and, though few, drove away the many barbarous nations that had their eyes on the country,

or the rebuilding of the magnificent temple, renowned throughout the whole world, or the great city’s attainment of complete freedom from everyone, or how the Lord God was pleased with us in all kindness, gentleness, and peace—
all these things that Jason of Cyrene set forth in five books, we will endeavor to present very briefly in this single account.
For we considered the great mass of words and the burden it would seem to impose on those wishing to delve into the contents of these books

and go over the same ground because of the density, substance, and depth of their words. We took care to provide enjoyment for readers, an effortless reminder for the learned, and an account free of distortion and corruption for everyone.
Do not consider the labor we undertook for this concise account an easy effort, or one requiring little sweat and toil.
Just as someone preparing to entertain invited friends gives a great banquet for his friends’ enjoyment and does not think of his own ease, so we undertook the labor for the pleasure of many.
We left precision and verification to the original writer; we did not delay in abridging, [?], and presenting the brief account in condensed form.

Just as, in the shared construction of a palace, the work is divided among many, but the beginning and completion of the buildings belong to the chief architect, while plastering, coloring, enameling, and painting belong to the decorator.

Likewise, our questioning, testing, investigation, pursuit of the truth of the accounts, and bringing profound matters to light through deep understanding are to be required of the one who took the lead in those writings.
But the brief, concise account, such as I have now undertaken to narrate, is to be required of me.

Now let us begin to recount what we have promised, adding only this much to what went before. Yet this too shows unreasonable thinking: to lengthen the introduction to the book while recounting the whole book briefly and concisely.
While the holy city was inhabited in complete peace and the laws were faithfully and admirably observed because of the devout, evil-hating holiness of Onias the high priest,
even the kings themselves were, as it were, obliged to honor the renowned temple with decrees, sacrifices, and many gifts.
Even Seleucus, king of the regions of Asia, supported the service of worship and paid from his own revenues all the expenses of the service for the burnt offerings.
A certain man named Simon, from the division of Bilgah, led his clan and came into conflict with the high priest over his own lawless conduct in the city.
When he could not prevail over Onias or accomplish anything, he came and stood before Apollonius, son of Thraseas, who at that time was commander of Lower Syria and Arabia.

And he told him that there were many treasures filling the treasury in Jerusalem, and that no one could even count or reckon the various kinds of treasure. He said that it ought to be placed under the king’s authority for use in the service of sacrifices.

Apollonius and the king undertook to disclose the treasures, as they had been reported to him. He summoned Heliodorus, his chief steward, and ordered him to remove this quantity of treasure and bring it from that city.

Heliodorus immediately set out and traveled on, under the pretext of touring the cities of Lower Syria and Arabia for instruction, but his real intention was to carry out the king’s command without delay.

When he arrived in Jerusalem, the high priest and the whole city welcomed him warmly and generously. He began to tell them what had been disclosed to the king, and said, “Who has accused you before the king, and why, or how? And is there really as much treasure as they said?”
The high priest stepped forward and said, “There are indeed deposits belonging to widows and orphans, placed here for safekeeping.

“There are also deposits belonging to Hyrcanus, a prominent man of the family of Tobias, but not as much as the accuser, that lawless letter-writer Simon, claimed. Altogether, even at a generous estimate, there are four hundred talents of silver and two hundred talents of gold.
“But there is no way to defraud those who have placed their trust in the great honor of this splendid temple, known throughout the world as secure and trustworthy.”
When he heard the high priest’s words, he brought up the royal command and said, “The command is that this treasure should go to the king’s service and use.”
He announced a day and hour for entering, counting, and taking it, and made preparations according to the royal command. There was no little distress and danger of unrest in the city.

The priests themselves fell down and rolled on the ground before the altar, still wearing their sacred robes. They implored the one who had established laws for the careful safeguarding of deposits to enable them to return these intact and unharmed to their respective depositors.
There one could see the high priest’s appearance and melt inwardly, for his appearance and the color of his face revealed the sorrow in his heart.
For fear and dread had descended upon him, clung to him, and surrounded and besieged him, and his body trembled. From all this, the anguish of his heart was evident to those who saw him.
From their respective houses, they came in groups to join in the prayers of all the people, so that the honor of the great temple would not be treated with contempt.
Women wearing sackcloth lamented in the public squares. Secluded virgins ran from their quarters to the doors and walls, while some leaned out through the windows.
And all together, with voices raised in prayer, they lifted their hands toward heaven and waved their fingers.

There was a pitiable sight to see: all the people falling down and rolling on the ground as they offered their prayers to heaven, with an extraordinarily great urgency of distress in keeping with the high priest’s fears.
And as they lay prostrate and rolled on the ground, they cried out to the Almighty that the deposits of those who had entrusted them might be returned to them intact and unharmed.
And Heliodorus encountered the verdict of the revelation. And while he was going about the treasury with his attendant,

He who holds power over souls and all authorities in his hands made a great and remarkable appearance, so that all who had dared to enter with him became weak, collapsed, and were paralyzed. By the power of God they were handed over to a miserable defeat.
there suddenly appeared to them a majestic horse with its rider, splendidly adorned and equipped with golden armor,
and two other men, powerful youths dressed in beautiful attire, stood before the rider. They quickly approached from the right and the left and struck Heliodorus with tremendous blows.
Until they carried him away, fallen, unconscious and senseless, close to death.
He who had entered and walked about the treasury with such splendor, honor, authority, and attendants was now lifted up and carried away in an unconscious state.
For the powers of God had plainly come upon him, and he lay thrown to the ground, half dead, speechless and voiceless, deprived of all hope of deliverance.

But those around Onias blessed the Lord, who glorified his holy places in every way. The temple, which a little earlier had been filled with turmoil, was filled with gladness, joy, and unceasing delight at the appearance of the glory of the almighty Lord.

Then some of those who had come with the commander, his well-disposed leading companions, hurried to the feet of Onias, begging him to ask the Most High to grant the man at least his life. For he lay so miserably stricken and wasted away, approaching his final hour.

The high priest considered that the king might suspect that the man had been harmed through some treachery on his part or on the part of the Jews. So he offered prayers and sacrifices for the man's deliverance.

Just as the atoning sacrifices were being offered by the high priest, the same young men immediately came down and stood before Heliodorus, arrayed in the same clothing. They said, “You must be deeply grateful to Onias the high priest, for because of him the Lord has granted you your life through him.
But you, having been punished with such suffering because of him, must tell everyone of the great might of God's powers.” When they had said this, they immediately disappeared.

When Heliodorus regained consciousness, he stood up and immediately offered burnt offerings to the Lord. He fulfilled great vows and prayers to the Lord, who had granted him his life and immediately restored his strength to its former measure. He honored Onias the high priest with great respect and generous gifts, and then set out and returned to the king.
Everywhere he spread accounts of God's wonders, bearing witness to what he himself had seen with his own eyes.

When the king began to question Heliodorus, saying, “How did it go? What did you accomplish in the task for which you went?” he began to recount it with lamentation and said, “Ah, let him indeed go to Jerusalem!
Whoever is your enemy and a threat to your great affairs, order that man to be sent there, and you will find him returning from there severely beaten, if he can even survive.

For a truly great power dwells there. He whose power extends to the highest heavens watches over that place and helps it. Whoever comes to that place with hostility or contempt, he strikes with terrible blows before letting him go—if he lets him go at all.”
This much was said concerning Heliodorus and the siege of the treasury building.

But Simon, who was secretary of the treasury and the province, became still more persistent in accusing Onias, saying that he himself was entirely responsible for attacking and tormenting Heliodorus, and that he was the instigator and perpetrator of every evil.
He dared to denounce the city's benefactor and guardian, the benefactor of the nation and the zealous defender of the laws, reproaching him as someone harmful to the king's interests.
He pursued his hostile rivalry and envy so far that he made the holy man deserving of death in the eyes of some whom Simon had set to work.

When Onias saw how unmanageable the opposition had become, he turned his attention to the wrongdoing of Apollonius, the commander of Lower Syria and Arabia. He too was joining Simon in his evil deeds, and they were inflaming the king's mind to such a degree.
He therefore considered it impossible to advance the common good without the king's help and orders.
Especially since he saw Simon incessantly and restlessly pursuing his schemes with cunning.

When Seleucus departed this world and Antiochus, surnamed Epiphanes, took the kingdom, a man named Jason, the brother of Onias, sought through corruption to enter the office and take the high priesthood away from Onias.
He promised to pay the royal treasury three hundred and sixty talents, and eighty talents from other revenues.

“I will also contribute another hundred,” he said, “if the undertaking succeeds. I will bring the city under your control, build theaters and arenas, and register the people of Jerusalem as Antiochenes in your name.”
When the king agreed, he obtained the authority he had requested. Immediately, step by step, he began turning their ancestral customs toward Greek paganism.

They abolished the earlier royal concessions, which had been secured through John and Ptolemy’s father during the embassy undertaken out of loving concern for the common welfare, as well as the lawful customs; and he introduced new, lawless regulations.
For he built theaters and training grounds for young men immediately below the citadel, and they selected vigorous youths and assigned them to instruction in athletic skills.
Thus they stirred up enthusiasm, setting in motion foreign customs and paganism because of the extreme delusion of the impious Jason, who was no true high priest.

For from then on, the service at the sacrificial altar and the duties of the temple were abandoned, and the burnt offerings were despised. The ranks of priests eagerly devoted themselves to wrestling and boxing, to the unlawful distributions for dancers, and to discus throwing and javelin throwing when the signal sounded.
They counted their ancestral honor as nothing, but considered the glory of lawless paganism better than the glory of blessing.

For this very reason, afflictions soon overtook them, surrounding them on every side and holding them under siege. For the very people whose habits and ways they envied, and whom they wished to resemble in everything, they themselves made into their own executioners, enemies, and torturers.
Let no one consider it a light matter to transgress God’s laws; the whole course of events that lies ahead will make this plain.
Now the time had arrived for the worship of the gods at the five-year festival in the city of Tyre, in the king’s presence.

For that ceremony, the lawless Jason sent competitors and festival participants from the holy city of Jerusalem, calling them Antiochenes. He entrusted them with three hundred staters for the cost of sacrifices in the worship of Vahagn. When the bearers arrived with the money, they begged that it not be used for sacrifices in the worship of idols, since it was neither right nor fitting for treasure from the holy place to go toward sacrifices in the worship of idol gods.

Those who received it accepted it for the purpose intended by the man who had sent it, namely, sacrificial worship. But because of the bearers’ plea, they did not use it for that purpose; instead, they put it toward the royal undertaking of paying for the construction of ships.

After the embassy of Apollonius, son of Menestheus, to the land of the Egyptians, Ptolemy, king of the Egyptians, passed away, and Antiochus took the crown in his place. Considering himself somewhat estranged from those regions, he turned back, set out, and came to the city of Joppa. From there he came to Jerusalem.
There he was greatly honored by Jason and the city, with magnificent displays, torches, and brilliantly blazing lights. Then he departed for the regions of Arabia with his entire army.
Then, after three years, Jason sent Menelaus, the brother of the frenzied Simon, entrusting him with the royal funds to take to the king.
When he appeared before the king and was honored by him, he began to secure the priesthood for himself. To outbid Jason, he added another three hundred talents to the payment to the treasury.
Having obtained the royal authorization to exercise authority, he came back. He did nothing worthy of the high priesthood, but behaved cruelly like a wild beast, displaying bitter rage.
Jason, who had treacherously usurped his own brother’s priesthood, in turn had that same priesthood taken from him by another. He fled as an exile to the land of the Ammonites.
Menelaus took control of the priesthood, but he could not pay in full what he had promised the king. The commander of the fortress began to press him urgently and demand payment.
For he was responsible for collecting the country's taxes. For this reason, both of them were summoned together to the royal court.
When Menelaus saw that he would not be able to pay the tax, he arranged for a replacement and appointed his brother Lysimachus in his place. Sostratus was in charge of the affairs of the Cypriots.
While these arrangements were in place, the people of Tarsus and Mallus happened to break out in open revolt, because they had been given over for the support of Antiochis, the king's concubine.
He hastened to set out, reach them, and subdue them, leaving Andronicus in his place with the same rank.
When Menelaus found a suitable opportunity, he secretly stole gold vessels from the temple and gave them to Andronicus. He had also sold other vessels in Tyre and in the surrounding cities.
Onias openly exposed this from the stronghold where he had taken refuge at Daphne near Antioch.

For this reason, Menelaus won Andronicus over to his side and urged him to seize Onias by force. Andronicus went to Onias and deceitfully offered him assurances, making solemn pledges to him with weighty oaths. He persuaded him to come out of the stronghold, although Onias was suspicious. As soon as he had brought him out, he murdered him, showing no regard at all for justice.
Because of this, not only the Jews but also the Gentiles were angry, especially because of the man's undeserved death.
But when the king returned from the regions of Cilicia, Jews and Gentiles from city after city came before him, grieving over the man who had been killed without cause and unjustly put to death.
At this, Antiochus was distressed in his heart, was moved to compassion, and wept greatly over the man's holiness and great wisdom.

He burned fiercely with anger and immediately ordered Andronicus's purple robes to be pulled off over his head. Andronicus was stripped of his clothing and led around the city. At the very place where the crime against Onias had been committed, he ordered the condemned criminal to be beheaded, the Lord bringing the punishment he deserved upon the evildoer.

When many secret thefts from the treasury were committed by Lysimachus with Menelaus's approval, and reports of them spread abroad, the people gathered against Lysimachus, for many gold vessels were counted as missing.

When the people began to press him and attack him in great anger, Lysimachus armed about three thousand men. He began to use force and initiate acts of violence, led by a man who was even more savage in appearance than he was dull in mind.

When they saw Lysimachus's treachery and deceit, they quickly gathered and took action. Some took stones, others clubs, and some sand and gravel mixed with earth, and together they hurled these at their attackers.

They sent some away wounded and others with their heads battered, killed many, and put them all to flight. They drove the very man who had stripped the altar and plundered the temple fleeing toward the treasury building.
Because of all this, legal proceedings were brought against Menelaus.
When the king came down to Tyre, the cases were heard before him, for three men from the council of elders of the people had come to present their case.
When Menelaus lost his case, he promised to give Ptolemy a large sum of money to win his favor.
For this reason, Ptolemy took the king aside under the pretext of taking a walk and changed his mind.

Menelaus, who was guilty of every evil, was released from the charges. But those unfortunate men, who would have been acquitted and gone away blameless even if they had pleaded their case before the Chaldeans, were condemned to death.
They immediately inflicted the punishment for injustice on those who had come to report the disaster concerning the city, the community, and the sacred vessels.
Because of all this, the people of Tyre, who hated wickedness, prepared their bodies for burial with deep sorrow.
They sent Menelaus away because of the rulers’ [?] and greed. Slander remained firmly established, and he inflicted great and murderous harm on his fellow citizens.
At the time of Antiochus’s second arrival in the land of the Egyptians, he sent [?] from the territory of the people of Antioch.
Throughout the city, for forty days, mounted spearmen in golden attire appeared between heaven and earth.

They were armed and arrayed, charging, attacking, and clashing with one another. There were the crash of shields, the twang of bows, the flash of swords, the rustling of standards, the whistling of arrows, and the gleam of golden armor.
Everyone fell down and prayed that these signs would turn out for good.

When a rumor suddenly burst forth that Antiochus had departed this world, Jason gathered no fewer than twenty thousand armed men and attacked the city. Because of the sudden treacherous attack, the people were driven back from the wall. Menelaus rushed ahead and reached the city.

There Jason, raging and merciless, fell upon his fellow citizens and carried out great massacres as though he were among enemies. He did not consider that he was turning the well-being of his own people and fellow citizens into misery. Instead, he thought he was repeatedly harrying enemies and raising a sign of victory over the company of his own people as though over an enemy.
He could not gain any power, however, and in the end inherited only the shame of his treachery. He himself fled to the territory of the Ammonites.

There he met a terrible end, having been imprisoned by Aretas, king of the Arabs. Again he became a fugitive from city to city, hated and pursued by everyone as a rebel against the laws, defiled and loathed as a betrayer and executioner of his country, city, and people. In the land of the Egyptians he raged and spat.
He drove countless people out of his own country, and he himself, an exile among foreigners, perished.
He was unmourned, uncared for, and unprepared for burial, and was not deemed worthy of his ancestral tombs.

When the king was informed of what had happened, he considered Judea to have rebelled against him. For this reason he hurried away from the land of the Egyptians and, with a heart turned savage, came against the city with the sharp edge of the sword and the point of the spear.
He ordered the soldiers to slaughter mercilessly those who fell into their hands and to kill inside the buildings those who took refuge there.
There children and old people alike were slaughtered, women and infants alike were destroyed, and virgins, male and female alike, were massacred.
In those three days they slaughtered eighty thousand altogether, and sold forty thousand, no fewer than those killed, for a good price.

And since he was not satisfied with these evils, he dared to lay hands on the holiest place in all the world. He dared to enter the temple, taking Menelaus as his guide, who had become a traitor and executioner to the laws, the country, and the people.

With impure and lawless hands they took the holy vessels of the altar and what other kings and other cities had dedicated to the sanctuary for the enhancement and glory of the place, and distributed them among the impure.

Perhaps Antiochus had become proud and obstinate in his mind and said, “The Lord of these people is angry because of the sins and lawlessness of the inhabitants of this city. That is why contempt has fallen upon the holy place.”

For if they had not been overwhelmed by great sins, it would have been as with Heliodorus, who was sent by King Seleucus to make an accounting of the treasury: this man too, upon entering, would immediately have been brought down because of his pride.
But the Lord did not choose the people for the sake of the place; he chose the place for the sake of the people.
For the place itself shared in the people’s waywardness, just as it would later share in their good fortune, when it once again found favor with the great God, in the glory of its restoration.

But Antiochus took eight hundred talents in addition to the nine hundred and carried them away from the temple. He quickly reached the city of Antioch, so proud in his thoughts that he imagined he could change the sea into dry land and dry land into sea.
He left harsh overseers there to torment the remaining inhabitants of Jerusalem, including Philip, a Phrygian by birth, who was even more savage in character than the man who left him there.
At Gerizim he left Andronicus, and over them he placed Menelaus, who ruled the city even more cruelly than they did.

But because he had a little pity for the Jews, he sent Apollonius of [?] with twenty thousand troops, not counting the first thousand, to slaughter all the men indiscriminately and sell the women and children.

When he came to Jerusalem, he first entered peacefully, using deceit, and remained there until the holy day, the Sabbath. When he found the Jews resting on the Sabbath, he ordered his troops to arm themselves.
He put to the sword everyone who came to see [?]. Fully armed, his troops ran here and there throughout the city, striking everyone down and leaving heaps of bodies.

But Judas Maccabeus, who was one of ten, fled into the wilderness and lived like a wild animal in the mountains. Together with the band who were with him, he spent his time eating wild plants, so that they would not come into contact with defilement.
After a long time, the king sent Athenobius, an old man, to compel and pressure the Jews to transgress the laws of their ancestors and no longer remain faithful to the laws of God,
and to defile the temple in Jerusalem and henceforth name it after Olympian Zeus, and the temple at Gerizim after Zeus, the hospitable giver of shelter, in keeping with those who lived in that place.
They brought upon them grievous and unbearable suffering through these evils.

They filled the holy temple with the contrived defilements of the pagans, and turned the sacred court into a place of filth through sexual intercourse between men and women. They boldly brought inside things that were utterly improper.
They filled the altar itself entirely with things that dishonored and were forbidden by the laws.
There it was impossible to observe the Sabbath laws or keep the ancestral annual festivals, and no one dared even to call himself a Jew.

They repeatedly drove them under compulsion to sacrifice at the monthly celebration of the king’s birthday. When the festival of the worship of Dionysus arrived, they forced them to dance, crowned with thick branches sacred to Dionysus.

They sent an order that officials should be stationed in all the neighboring towns and, as the people of Ptolemais had proposed, that wherever they went, people should perform the rites with sacrifices.
Those who refused to sacrifice were to be put to the sword on the spot. There one could see the desperate distress and suffering of those being tortured.

A written accusation was made against two women for circumcising their sons. They were brought forward at once, and the children were hung from their mothers’ breasts. The women were paraded through the public squares in mockery, and then thrown down from the walls.

Others secretly went to nearby caves to spend the Sabbath days. When they were discovered, they were killed by being burned alive, on account of their reverence for the day of rest and the holiness of the laws.
But I beg all of you who read this book not to lose heart over our nation, and not to consider all these afflictions as intended to destroy our people, but to discipline our nation.
He does not leave the lawless unpunished for long, but quickly makes his signs and his deeds known.
For it is not the case that, just as God is patient with the other nations until they fill up the measure of their sins and come under inescapable judgments,
he also deals with us in the same way, allowing us to reach the point of judgment.
Rather, he disciplines us continually and swiftly brings mercy upon us.
We have spoken these words to you as a reminder of these matters. Now let us return to the main course of the narrative.
Eleazar, a distinguished man among the foremost in that company, full of years, advanced in age, and handsome in appearance, was being forced to eat pork, with a [?] put into his mouth.

He had resolved, with a steadfast and determined heart, to accept death with an honorable name rather than a life burdened by remorse and the reproaches of his companions. He willingly chose to undergo torture, boldly spitting upon and dishonoring their rites.
This is fitting for those who endure: openly to reject what it is unlawful for them to partake of.

Those who had come prepared to conduct the sacrifices, out of weakness of mind and selfish inclinations, were also acquainted with the elderly man. Taking him aside, they tried, with their own weak understanding, to turn his steadfast mind toward the enticements of indulgence. They said, “Accept the king’s command,
and we will serve you different meat, so that you may dispel suspicion and escape death.”

But he had established a noble resolve within himself, worthy of his age, of the dignity of his old age, of his distinguished appearance, of his luxuriant, radiant gray hair, and of his excellent upbringing from childhood to advanced age. Above all, it accorded with the God-given holiness of his law-giving religion, complete in all its ordinances. He promptly gave his answer.

“It is neither worthy nor fitting,” he said, “at our age to introduce hypocrisy into the confession of holiness. Many of those young people may see it, form suspicions in their minds, and say, ‘Eleazar, more than ninety years old and standing at death’s door, has turned to the ways of foreigners.’
They would stumble because of my hypocrisy, and I would leave behind in the world this burden on my conscience and a tarnished name for my old age.
Even if they grant me just as much time to live again, and I am never again delivered into human hands, I can never escape the eternal, everlasting hands, either while alive or after death.
Therefore I will depart courageously from this world, so that I may show myself worthy of my old age.

I will leave the young an example of goodness and virtue, so that they may be able to struggle willingly and courageously for the holiness of the laws, even to the point of death.” When he had said all this, he willingly and resolutely went forward to the suffering of death and torture.

Those who had previously gathered around him to console him turned their words of consolation into hostility. They considered his wise reasoning to be folly and pressed him all the more severely with torture.

When he was close to death from the tortures, he opened his mouth and, groaning, began to speak to the Lord, who knows the mysteries of holiness. He said, “This one thing has become clear: although it was in my power to escape the pains of death, I endure these harsh tortures inflicted on my body. Yet in my soul I accept them courageously and gladly, out of fear of the Lord’s threats.”
Having fought in this way, he departed from this world.
It happened that seven brothers were arrested together with their mother and brought before the king’s tribunal. Through torture and beatings, they were being forced to eat pork.

One of them came forward first to face the struggle. He began to speak and said, “Why do you stand aside, and what are you going to ask us? We are ready to die rather than transgress our ancestral laws.”

The king was filled with anger and fury. He ordered frying pans and cauldrons to be heated, and wheels and various instruments of torture to be prepared. When these had quickly been heated and prepared,

he ordered the one who had come forward to be brought before him. First they cut out his tongue and stripped the skin from his head and face. Then they cut off his hands and feet in front of his mother and brothers.

Then, when he had been rendered unable to speak or use his hands, the king ordered him to be lowered alive into the heated frying pans. As the fumes rose from the pan in a long, towering column, the brothers, together with their mother, began to encourage one another, saying, “Let us die courageously and inherit the name and the souls [?].”
“The Lord God watches the struggle of our battle and has compassion on his servants, as Moses plainly declared in his blessing: ‘He has compassion on his servants.’”

When the first had departed from this world in this way, they brought the second to the place of torture. They stripped the skin from his head and face, together with his hair, and immediately asked him, “Will you eat pork before your whole body is torn apart limb by limb?”
He answered them in their own language and said, “No.” Because of this, he too was tortured with the same torments and died.

When he was about to give up his spirit, he began to speak and said to the king, “You arrogant, proud, and insolent man! You think you are cutting us off from this present earthly life. But the King of the worlds, though we die for his laws, will restore us to eternal life at the time when we are born anew.”
After him they brought the third and demanded his tongue. He immediately offered it and courageously stretched out his hands.
Even the king himself marveled at the young man’s presence of mind and courage of heart, because he regarded the pain as nothing.
When he passed away, they brought the fourth forward in his place and subjected him to the same tortures.

When his breath was nearing its end, he began to speak as follows: “It is better for us to depart from here at human hands, looking forward in hope to being born anew in the resurrection of the dead, than for you to remain alive, because the resurrection of the dead is barred and shut to you.”
After him they brought the fifth to the painful tortures. He raised his eyes, looked at the king, and began to speak to him, saying:

Having gained authority over people, you too, though a mortal man, do whatever you please. But do not think that through any wickedness you can cut off our nation, or regard it as abandoned and left out of God's hands.
“Wait, and you will see the power of his great wonders, how he will torment you and your family with terrible blows.”

After this the sixth was brought forward. When he was close to death, he said, “Why are you vainly deceived about us? These things that are happening are because of our sins, for we have sinned against God. This is worthy of wonder [?].”
“But do not expect to survive unharmed and at ease after setting yourself against God.”
Still more worthy of honorable remembrance was the remarkable mother, who lost seven such sons of her own in one day, at one time, because of her hope in God.
Encouraged and strengthened in heart, she encouraged and comforted each of them in their own language, kindling her heart and mind with manly strength.

Stepping forward courageously, she said, “I do not know how you all appeared in my womb. I did not give you your spirits or your lives, nor did I fashion each of your forms. Though I gave birth to you and nourished you as you grew, from now on I will count nothing as my own.
Rather, the Creator of the world, who brought humankind into being, will, at his coming, restore your lives and your spirits to you in his mercy.”

Although Antiochus considered himself scorned because of the martyrs’ language, nevertheless, while the youngest child was still alive, he began not only to offer encouragement with words but also to assure him with concrete promises that he would raise him to greatness and high rank and make him prosperous in the world, provided only that he turned away from his ancestral laws. He would give him an office and call him a friend of kings.
When the king saw that the young man was not swayed at all by his words, he called the mother and begged her to counsel the young man for the sake of his life, so that he might be saved.
When he pressed her very insistently, she agreed to speak with her son and bent down toward him.

She began to mock the proud, arrogant king and said, “Have pity on me, my son. Remember that I carried you in my womb for nine months, held you in my arms and nursed you at my breasts for three years, and brought you up to your present stature.
Now I beg you, my son, look at heaven and earth and all the creatures in them. Remember that God made them out of nothing, and that the human race was likewise created by him.

Do not be terrified of that sinister executioner. Instead, prove yourself worthy of your brothers and choose death over life in this world, so that I may receive you with those brothers into the merciful hands of the great God.”

While his mother was offering these words of encouragement to strengthen his resolve, the young man began to speak and said, “Whom are you waiting for? Why are you delaying? I will not obey your king’s command. Instead, I obey the commands of our fathers’ laws, which were given through Moses.
But you, who have devised all these evils against the children of the Hebrews, will not escape the hands of God.
For even if, as a punishment to correct us,
our living Lord has been angry for a little while, he will again show favor and mercy to his servants.
But you, lawless rebel, filthy coward, why do you vainly exalt yourself over his servants with your empty hope?
You will certainly not escape the judgment of the all-knowing, almighty God.
For now our brothers, having endured a little suffering for eternal life and for the covenant of God’s testaments, lie fallen and stretched out in death.

But I, like my brothers, am ready to surrender my life and body for the laws of our fathers. In hope I call upon God, asking that the whole nation may find forgiveness, and that through severe tortures and groaning you may confess that he alone is God and there is no other;
and that through me and my brothers all the wrath and anger that have built up may be wiped away and brought to an end.”
The king was crushed by such courage of heart in the seven children, and they inflicted especially bitter tortures on the youngest.
Yet he too departed from this world undefiled and holy, trusting in the Lord.
After her sons, the blessed mother also met her end in the same manner.
Let what has been related thus far stand concerning the questioning about sacrifices and the unbearable tortures.

But Judas Maccabeus and those with him secretly entered villages, cities, and farms here and there, gathering their fellow countrymen around him. He rallied the Jews who had remained steadfast in their covenant. They formed a band, increased in number, and grew to about six thousand men.
They called upon the Lord to visit and look upon the people who had been trampled by the nations, and to have compassion on the temple that had been defiled by impious hands;
to have mercy on the city that was about to be ruined and destroyed to its foundations, and to heed the cry of the blood;
to remember the unjust destruction of innocent children, and to take to heart the blasphemies against his holy name.
When Maccabeus had assembled his army, the nations could not stand against him, for the fierce anger of the divine majesty had turned to mercy.
He attacked villages and cities, set fire to the enemies’ fortified strongholds, subdued them, brought back those captured by the enemies, and inflicted great and severe blows on the enemy.
He found the night especially helpful as his ally, and the fame of his courage spread in every direction.

When Philip saw that the man’s undertakings were advancing successfully time after time, he sent messengers with royal letters to Ptolemy, the commander of Coele-Syria and Arabia, asking him to provide troops as reinforcements.

As soon as he received the letters, he put Nicanor, son of Patroclus, one of the foremost of his trusted dignitaries, in command of no fewer than forty thousand men, to wipe out the Jewish nation completely. He assigned to him Gorgias, a commander who was a brave man, experienced in warfare and skilled in every aspect of it.
Nicanor undertook to make up the outstanding tribute paid to the Romans, one hundred talents, from the sale of Jewish captives.

He sent orders around the coastal regions, inviting slave merchants to Judea and promising to give them ninety people for one talent. He paid no attention to the judgment from heaven that the Almighty had already prepared against him.
There were some who informed Judas about Nicanor’s advance.
In their faintheartedness, they fled here and there.

They sold whatever they had left, and together they begged the Almighty Lord to save them from the lawless and unworthy hand of Nicanor, who, before he had even seen them, had agreed with the merchants on the prices for their persons.

Even if not for their own sake, they asked him nevertheless to deliver them from Nicanor for the sake of the covenants and agreements with their fathers, and for the sake of his own great and holy name.

Maccabeus assembled those with him, about six thousand men, and encouraged them not to be dismayed by so great a multitude of troops, nor to lose heart before the mass of the army of the nations that had gathered to attack them without cause, but to stand and fight bravely.
He urged them to take to heart the outrage committed against the holy place, the sufferings of the city struck by captivity, and the destruction of the sacred laws of their ancestors.

“They,” he said, “trust in weapons and in their own strength, but we trust in Almighty God, who can destroy both those who set their sights on us and the whole world with a single breath of his power.”

He began to remind them, one by one, of the courageous deeds of those in earlier times and of the help that had come from the Lord. “Remember Sennacherib and the destruction of one hundred and eighty thousand men at once.”

Remember the war of the Romans against the Galatians: the latter had all gone into battle together, numbering one hundred and twenty thousand. The Romans went out with six thousand and, at one time, slaughtered all one hundred and twenty thousand, filled with help from the Most High.
With these words of comfort he encouraged them, stirred them up, and prepared them to fight resolutely for their laws and their country and to die boldly.
He divided the army into three divisions and appointed his two brothers, Simon and Joseph, as commanders of two of the divisions.

Again, to encourage and comfort the soldiers, he brought out the sacred books of Ezra and read them aloud before them. He gave each of the soldiers a sign in the name of the Lord. Taking command of the first division himself, he advanced and attacked Nicanor.

When help from the Almighty descended upon them, they advanced and struck the enemy troops, killing more than nine thousand armed men in their first assault. They left others wounded, maimed, and injured, and posted guards around the camp.
They took for themselves the possessions and money of the merchants who bought people, and put Nicanor’s remaining troops to flight before them until it grew late in the day.
When the hour grew late, they hurried back at once and did not pursue them far, because the next day was the Sabbath.

Returning, they occupied the battlefield, gathered the weapons of the fallen, stripped the wounded, and prepared themselves for the Sabbath. They blessed, gave thanks to, and glorified the Lord, because he had saved them from their enemies that day. They made that day a day of mercy and a sign of victory.
After the Sabbath, they gave the afflicted, the widows, and the orphans a share of the spoils, and then took their own shares of the spoils.
When they had done this, they all fell down together and offered prayers to the merciful God, asking him to remain gracious toward his servants to the end.

In the battle they fought against Timothy and Bacchides, they advanced, clashed with them, struck them, and killed more than twenty thousand of their men. They courageously took possession of many strongholds and heights. They carried off much of their wealth and possessions as plunder, and gave the poor, the orphans, and the elderly a share in their spoils.
They gathered the weapons of those who had been killed and left them in suitable places. They themselves came to Jerusalem with the spoils, to the leaders of the tribes.
There they killed Timothy, who had inflicted many sufferings upon the Jewish people.

They gathered the people of the districts, made a day of rejoicing, and set up a sign of victory. They brought in the fugitive Callisthenes and those who were with him, whose gates he had set on fire, and burned him alive.
But Nicanor, who had suffered disaster on every side and had brought a thousand merchants to buy the children of the Jews,

fell into great suffering and misery. Stripped of his splendid clothing at the Lord’s command, dressed in rags and reduced to the company of beggars, deeply mourning the destruction of his army, he fled in humiliation and arrived in the city of Antioch.

And the man who had promised to pay the tribute to the Romans with the captives of Jerusalem now declared with his own mouth that God was plainly their helper. For this reason they came out of battle unharmed and without wounds, because they steadfastly kept the laws they had received from him.

At that time Antiochus happened to return from the regions of Persia in great disgrace. He had gone to the city in their heartland and planned to seize its treasury; if possible, he also intended to destroy the city itself. When the city's forces learned of this, they all rushed to arms and drove away from them, shamefully and with his head bowed, the man who had attacked them with such ferocity.
As Antiochus departed and traveled away from the regions of Persia in shame, he reached the region of Ecbatana, where he was informed of the events that had befallen him.
He recalled the insolence of the citizens who had put him to flight.

Filled with anger at both places, he resolved to vent his furious anger on the people of Jerusalem. For this reason he ordered his charioteer to drive rapidly, urgently, and without stopping, intent on the journey. He gave no thought to judgment coming from heaven, but swelled greatly with pride and arrogance and declared that he would leave Jerusalem empty of Jews.

But the almighty Most High, the Lord God of Israel, struck him with invisible blows. While the words were still in his mouth, severe and unbearable pains came upon his bones, and bitter cramps seized his belly.
It was entirely just that the man who had inflicted many strange and grievous pains on the bodies of others through torture should himself be seized and held captive by pains of the same severity.

Even so, he did not abandon his pride but burned still more fiercely with arrogance and anger against the Hebrews, urging haste along the road. Then, as he was traveling at speed, he fell from his chariot. He fell into grievous torment, for all his bones were shattered.

The man who had just imagined that, in his lawless pride, he could command the waves of the sea, bring the mountain heights low, and raise the low places high, was himself cast to the ground and carried about on others' backs, as the power of God was openly revealed.
Swarms of worms came pouring from the lawless man's eyes, and while he was still alive, the suffering caused by his disease tore his limbs apart. The stench of his decay distressed the entire army.
The man who had previously imagined in his proud mind that he could gather up the stars of heaven could now find no one able to carry him about, because of the unbearable stench of his decay.
Then he began to break free of his proud, arrogant stubbornness and come to his senses under God's torments, as pains struck his inflamed body one after another.
Since he himself could not endure the stench of his decay, he began to say, “It is right and fitting to submit to the Lord God and not, in a mortal body, exalt oneself as though one were a god.”
He pleaded and made vows to the one who would not show him mercy.
Instead of leveling the holy city to the ground and leaving it deserted, he vowed to make it populous and free.

He vowed that the Hebrews, whom he had threatened to deny both shrouds and burial, exposing them with their wives and children as food for birds and leaving them to be torn apart by wild beasts, would become his fellow citizens, equal to the Athenians, by written decrees.

And the holy temple, which I previously threatened to leave plundered and stripped, I will adorn with splendid offerings. I will return many times over the ornaments and utensils of the temple that were previously taken away, and provide from the royal treasury the regular revenues needed for the sacrifices.
Beyond all this, he vowed to become a Hebrew himself and to go to every inhabited place, proclaiming the power of God's greatness.

Since there was no way for his pains to cease—for punishment had come upon him from the Lord by a just judgment—and since he no longer held any hope of surviving, he wrote a letter to the Hebrews with great humility, in the following form:
“Warmest greetings to the beloved Hebrews, my friends, brothers, and fellow citizens.
I am deeply grateful to God for you.”

In my weakness, suffering from an incurable illness, I remembered you with great affection. I have returned from the regions of Persia and fallen into a severe illness. So I thought it good to do this for the benefit and welfare of all.
It is not that I have given up hope of living; rather, I expect to recover from this severe illness.
But I also considered how my father, when he set out on a journey to the upper regions, designated his successor,
so that, if anything happened to him or any troubling report arrived, they would know to whose keeping and charge his position had been entrusted and would not be disturbed.

With this in mind, I made known to those around us, the intimates of our kingdom, and those around us who looked to us with expectation, that my son Antiochus would take my place as king. Many times already, when I set out and traveled to the upper regions, I entrusted him to many of you and left him in your hands before departing. I have also written to them a copy of the letter that I have written to you below.
Now I ask you to remember the favors and benefits given to all, and the love and help given to each of you, and to maintain your harmonious allegiance to me and to my son.
For I know this with firm confidence: following the example of my conduct, he will treat you even more kindly and humanely.
Thus the savage, lawless blasphemer fell and was brought to ruin, dying in foreign mountains. With the cruel torments that he had inflicted on others, he was cut off from life.
Philip, his foster brother, who took his body away, was afraid of his son and fled to Ptolemy in the land of the Egyptians.
Maccabeus and those with him, strengthened by the Lord’s help, recovered the city and the temple.
They demolished the altars in the city that had been made by foreigners, together with the places of worship.

They purified the temple and built another altar, purifying the stones with fire. Then they again took fire from them and offered burnt sacrifices after an interval of two years, lit lamps, offered incense, and set out the continual offerings of bread in abundance.

When they had done this, they fell down, lying on their faces, and begged the Lord that the same evils might not befall them again. Even if they should ever commit some sin, they asked him to discipline them gently by his own hand and not to hand us over to blasphemous, savage nations.

Now it happened that the sanctuary was restored on the very same day, at the same time, on which the temple had been defiled at the hands of the Gentiles: on the twenty-fifth of the month called Chislev.

They celebrated the festival joyfully and gladly for eight days, in the manner of the days of the Festival of Booths, so that they might remember how previously they had observed the Festival of Booths in the mountains, in caves and rocky clefts, roaming like grazing animals.
For this reason, taking beautiful branches from leafy trees and palm branches, [?] to the one who had enabled them to purify his own place.
We ordered these days to be observed as an annual festival of feasting, with joy and gladness, by the common decision of the Hebrew nation, and this annual festival to be included in their calendar.
So much, then, concerning the death of Antiochus, called Epiphanes.
But concerning Antiochus Eupator, the offspring of the lawless man, we will briefly recount the events that befell the cities.
When Antiochus received the crown, he appointed Lysias over the royal affairs of the regions of Lower Syria and Arabia.

Ptolemy, who was called the Tall, firmly upheld justice toward the Hebrews. Because of the covenants that had been made and the rights of which they had been deprived, he strove to deal with them peacefully.

For this reason his associates accused him before Antiochus and called him a traitor, because the regions of Cyprus had been in his charge by order of Philometor, but he had abandoned him and come to Antiochus. Unable to endure the insults, he took poison himself and died.
Gorgias, the commander of the region, gathered troops together with the Edomites to advance, attack, and scour the strongly fortified districts.
They infiltrated and made incursions to drive them out of Jerusalem. They formed a fighting force and prepared for battle.
But those with Maccabeus offered prayers to God and called on him as their helper, so that they themselves might strike first against the Edomites’ strongholds.

When they arrived, they surrounded them, massed together, and attacked them all at once. They demolished the strongholds, struck down and slaughtered their occupants, and killed everyone they captured.
Some escaped and took refuge in two strong fortresses. They had all their equipment for war engines with them. They stationed guards around them and set up the engines along the walls.
Maccabeus left Simon, Joseph, Zacchaeus, and the troops with them to besiege the fortresses, and he himself departed.

But Simon’s men, who were stationed around the fortress, entered into negotiations and accepted bribes. They received seventy thousand double silver staters from those inside the fortifications and allowed them to come out and disperse.
When Maccabeus was informed of what had happened, he assembled all the leaders and accused them, declaring that they had sold their brothers for silver and released their enemies.
They brought those who had acted as traitors in this way to judgment under the law and put them to death. Then they themselves advanced against the fortress.
They reached it, surrounded it, and besieged it, for success was coming through his efforts. On that day they slaughtered more than twenty thousand.

Timothy, who had previously suffered defeat at the hands of the Hebrews, again took heart and gathered an army. He assembled many Asian cavalrymen from foreign regions and set out, intending to subject the land of Judea to captivity at spearpoint.
As they approached, those with Maccabeus persevered in prayer to God, putting earth on their heads and clothing themselves in sackcloth.

Falling before the altar, they rolled upon the steps and begged him henceforth to be reconciled with them, to drive away their enemies, and to stand against their adversaries. They offered all their prayers as the laws commanded.

When they had all finished their prayers, they turned to their weapons, armed and equipped themselves, and made ready. They went out beyond the city in full force. When they came near the enemy army, they arranged and equipped themselves and took up their battle formation in proper order.

Just as the rose-colored sun, red at its rim, was about to spread its light over the earth, the two sides joined battle. For one side, the day, made ready with favorable signs and gladness, joyfully offered victory: the glorious powers of the Lord’s heavenly aid descended in their light, surrounded them, and kept them firmly protected. For the other side, furious anger, driven and strengthened by their commanders’ pride, brought them to the battlefield in haste and turmoil.

Just as he was beginning to set the unsparing, merciless hand of war to work, five mounted men appeared from heaven, fully armed with golden weapons and golden adornments. They came down beside the enemy army and moved into the ranks of the Hebrews.

They surrounded Judas Maccabeus and advanced, covering him with their armor and taking him farther forward than his own armor could. They deflected all the arrows and spears coming against him from every side. With their own arrows, full of wrath, they struck the enemies directly in the eyes and blinded them all. The enemy troops fell into confusion and collided with one another.
Then, on that day, twenty thousand five hundred fully armed men from the enemy army were found fallen before them.
Timothy himself escaped through the crowd and fled. He reached Gazara, a fortified city where Chaereas was commander.
Maccabeus came with his troops, blockaded the fortress, and besieged it for four days.
But those inside, trusting in the strength of the city, mocked and ridiculed the Hebrews and, out of their own malice, hurled bitter insults at them.

As the fifth day of the week was about to dawn, twenty chosen men from the Hebrews’ force, together with Maccabeus, took up their weapons, filled with fierce indignation, and boldly charged through the city gate like wild beasts. They slaughtered at their feet those whom they found at the gate.

The troops all together attacked around the walls and raised such an uproar and shouting against the city that the soldiers guarding the walls above were hurled down from above, some inside and some outside, more thickly and swiftly than [?] a downpour. The attackers themselves rushed inside together and set fire to the fortress towers and all the wooden structures in the city. They burned the gates and the siege engines and destroyed all the visible and visible equipment. Then they built bonfires in the middle of the city and burned the blasphemers and those who had insulted them.

They took possession of all the goods and property, laws and institutions of that city, until they came upon Timothy, who had fled and hidden in a pit. They cut his throat, along with his brother Chaereas and Apollophanes, in that same pit.

When they had accomplished all this, they celebrated with blessing, rejoicing, thanksgiving, and gladness, praising the Lord, who with great might and a glorious name had brought victory through the hand of Israel.
A short time later, when Lysias, the king’s commander, heard about this, he was filled with great anger and indignation and was deeply distressed over what had happened.

He gathered an army, assembling eighty thousand men, and took all the troops with him, together with eighty thousand cavalry. Taking them with him, he marched against the Hebrews, intending to make the city the principal dwelling place of the Gentiles.
He also intended to make the holy temple a source of revenue by leasing it out like the other pagan temples, and to make the high priesthood itself an office rented from the treasury year by year.
He gave no thought to the power of God. Proud in his thoughts, he brought along tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry, and elephants massed together.

But when he pushed into Judea and approached the stronghold of Beth-zur, which is about five stadia from Jerusalem, he surrounded it with his tens of thousands and brought the stronghold into great distress.
When the Maccabees were informed of the siege of their stronghold, they fell down with the people, with lamentations and tears, and begged God to send a good angel to save the Israelites.
Maccabeus himself was the first to take up arms. He ordered the troops to arm themselves, equip themselves, prepare, and undertake the hardship of going to help their brothers who were in distress.

Then, united and of one mind, they armed themselves, made ready, and advanced. Just as they were approaching the vicinity of the city of Jerusalem, a man riding a white horse came down before them, armed with golden weapons. He brandished his spear and prepared to charge.

All together they raised a shout of encouragement and blessed the merciful God. They were so heartened and strengthened that they advanced to attack, resolved not merely to strike down human opponents, but, even if they encountered fearsome beasts or iron walls, to strike, destroy, overthrow, and break through them.
They charged boldly, having received the heavenly warrior as their companion in battle through his mercy.

And so, fierce as wild boars and like lions, they charged against the enemy army, and there, on that very spot, they struck down eleven thousand picked soldiers and a thousand horsemen in addition to those thousands.
They put the entire army to flight, and many of them escaped as wounded, injured, helpless, naked fugitives. Lysias himself fled headlong and barely escaped with his life.

He was not unaware of his own failure. Reflecting on it, he said that victory was impossible, saying that the mighty God was the Hebrews’ helper. He sent them away and sent after them to make peace on every just condition.
The king also agreed, and he won the king’s approval to be his friend.
Judas agreed to everything Lysias asked of him for the benefit of their common covenant arrangements, and everything that Maccabeus wrote to Lysias concerning the Jews, the king granted them.
Letters were written to the Jews in this form: “Lysias to the army of the Jews, greetings.
John and Absalom, whom you sent to us, presented us with the letter as coming from you and requested what was written in it. Whatever it was proper to grant, I granted,
and whatever needed to be brought before the king, I brought before him, so that permission might be given you concerning your affairs.
As for what was written to us, let there be goodwill between us and you. From now on I will strive still more to bring you benefits.
Concerning anything further, we have given instructions to speak with you.
Farewell. In the one hundred and forty-eighth year, on the festival of Hormizd, on the twenty-fourth day.”
The royal letter was written as follows: “King Antiochus to his brother Lysias, greetings.
Since our father was transferred to the service of the gods, we have wished that those under our kingdom should be free from disturbance.
Who more than these Jews? For at first they were not pleased with our father’s move toward paganism, and for this reason they asked for permission to observe their own laws.

We agreed and ordered that this nation should also be free from disturbance, that their temple should be returned to them, and that they should be treated kindly according to the laws of their ancestors.

Now you will do well and rightly to send to them, make a covenant, and conclude agreements, so that they may know our goodwill and care for them, take courage, and go about with greater peace of mind, having secured support for their own laws.”
The royal letter was written in this form: “King Antiochus to the council of elders of the Jews, to their forces, and to the companies of the Jews, warm greetings.
May you be well, and may everything be as we wish. We ourselves are also well.
Lysias informed us that you wish to go down to the Jews who are in Jerusalem.
Those who have now departed are to have until the thirtieth of the month of Ahekan; a pledge is to be given and agreements confirmed.
With forgiveness, relief, and kindness toward the Jews, let them remain in their own laws and religious observances as before, and let no one trouble them in any way.
We have sent Lysias and Menelaus to reassure you. Farewell.
In the one hundred and forty-eighth year, in the month of Ahekan, on the fifteenth day.”
The Romans also sent a letter in this form: “Quintus Memmius and Titus Manius, leaders of the Romans, to the people of the Hebrews, greetings.
We too approve the concessions that Lysias, the king’s brother, has granted you.

As for anything that ought to be presented to the king by us, consider it wisely and have it brought as quickly as possible, so that we may establish an arrangement that will benefit you as it should. For we are now going ahead to the city of Antioch.
Therefore hurry and send someone, so that we too may know what your intentions are.
Farewell. This treaty was concluded in the one hundred and forty-eighth year, at the festival of Hormizd.
Lysias went back to the king, and the Jews returned to their work, their plowing, and their crops.
The commanders of the armies—Timothy, Apollonius son of Gennaeus, Hieronymus, Demophon, and, besides these, Nicanor—gave them no relief or rest at all.
But the people of Joppa dared to commit this lawless act: spokesmen came and urged the Jews living among them to embark in boats with their wives and children,

with the unanimous agreement of the whole city. They undertook to bring them aboard as though in peaceful fellowship. The Jews accepted, having no suspicion or misgiving in their minds. They took them out and drowned them in the sea—no fewer than two hundred people.
When Judas learned of the harm caused by this lawless recklessness, he ordered the troops with him to call upon the righteous Judge.
He immediately came against those murderers. During the night they set fire to the harbor and burned the boats, and they struck down on the spot those who had taken refuge there.
After shutting up the strongholds as a security precaution, he withdrew and waited for an opportunity to return and destroy the entire population of Joppa.
He also came against the people of Jamnia, since they intended to do the same thing to their Hebrew fellow citizens.

He came against the people of Jamnia at night and set fire to the harbor, together with the boats, so that the glow of the fire could be seen in Jerusalem, which was about four hundred and eighty stadia away.
From there they advanced about twenty stadia against Timothy. As they were about to attack him, about five thousand Arabs and five hundred horsemen confronted him.

When the battle grew fierce, the forces clashed with one another. Judas’s force, trusting in the Lord’s help, saw before their eyes the favorable sign of victory. When the pastoral tribes were defeated, they approached Judas’s force, submitted, fell before them, and asked to establish a treaty. They also promised to give them livestock and to be useful to them in many matters.

Judas considered that there were many matters in which they could be useful to them. He agreed, granted them pardon, and made peace with them. Once they had established the treaty, they dispersed to their respective camps.
They made a raid against a city in that region called Caspin, fortified with walls and inhabited by troops of various nations. They surrounded it and kept it under siege.

Those inside trusted in the strength of the walls and looked to their abundant supplies. They regarded Judas and his troops with great arrogance and contempt, abusing them with bitter insults and saying things that ought not to have been said.

But they called for help upon the almighty, great, and powerful Lord of heaven and earth, who had destroyed Jericho without battering rams, catapults, or siege engines in the days of Joshua son of Nun. They gathered together and rushed against the walls like wild beasts.

They arrived and took the fortified city by the will of God. There they slaughtered so many of its troops that even the lake surrounding it, which measured about two stadia, appeared mingled with blood.
From there they set out and traveled toward Charax, about five hundred and fifty stadia away, approaching the Jews called Tobian Jews.
There they found Timothy, with none of his undertakings succeeding, weakened and deserted by his forces. However, he had left troops as guards in a strongly fortified place.

Then Dositheus and Sosipater, mighty men and commanders from the Maccabean army, went out with their troops. As they moved about with their force, they came upon that stronghold, attacked it, and slaughtered more than ten thousand men there.
Maccabeus divided the entire army into companies, and he himself advanced against Timothy with his own company. With Timothy were 120,000 troops carrying shields and about 2,500 cavalry.

When Timothy learned of the Maccabeans’ advance against him, he immediately sent the possessions and treasure, and the wives and children of the soldiers with him, to the stronghold of the people of Carnaim. The stronghold itself was impossible to besiege because the fortified terrain was narrow and difficult to approach.

But when Judas’s force appeared, advancing in great numbers, the enemy troops began to lose heart because dread of the Almighty had fallen upon them. They immediately fell into turmoil and confusion among themselves and turned to flee in every direction. Many, driven senseless by fear, ran onto their own weapons.
Judas’s force pressed fiercely upon the fugitives in relentless pursuit, wounding and striking them down together. In that place they laid low about thirty thousand fighting men from the army.

Timothy himself encountered the force of Dositheus and Sosipater. Having fallen into their hands, he earnestly begged them to spare his life, saying, “For [?] the relatives and brothers of many of you are with us. I will release them all to you, alive and unharmed, in exchange for my own life.”
After securing his promise to release many in exchange for himself, they let him go for the sake of rescuing their brothers.
When he got away and reached the stronghold, [?] he attacked and slaughtered more than twenty thousand of the people whom he had promised to release.

Immediately afterward they advanced against a fortified city named Ephron, where Lysias himself lived. Many [?] stood outside the walls, relying on the stronghold, the equipment of their projectile engines, and their ready weapons. Confident in their position, they fought outward from within.

But these men called for help upon the mighty Almighty, who can shatter the strength of those who wage war. They quickly took possession of the city and its fortifications. Inside it they struck down and slaughtered about twenty-five thousand men.
From there they made an incursion against the city of the Scythopolitans, about six hundred stadia from Jerusalem, whose people considered themselves benefactors of the Jewish nation.
The Jews who lived within the city also testified to the kindness they had received from its citizens during their time of distress.

When a peaceful encounter with the Maccabean force had been secured, they called out to the force that from then on they would show even greater loyalty to their people. The Maccabeans passed them by and hurried to the city of Jerusalem, because the festival marking the seventh week was drawing near.
When the feast of Pentecost was over, they marched against Gorgias, who was governor of the regions of the Edomites.
