He came out to meet them with thirty thousand shield-bearing soldiers and a force of four thousand cavalry.
When the two sides drew up their battle lines against one another, a few men from the Hebrew force happened to fall between the two battle lines.

A man named Dositheus, from the contingent of the Tobacenians, a strong, fully armed warrior, charged at Gorgias. Just as he was about to capture the lawless man, bind him, and present him as an offering before the Maccabean force, an armed soldier from the Thracian contingent struck his shoulder, dragged him down, and rescued Gorgias from his hands. Gorgias narrowly escaped and fled to the fortress of Mimara.
But as the battle of Ezra and his men dragged on and many were killed, the Maccabean force called upon the almighty, all-ruling God to come to their aid, appear, and lead the battle.
Thus, raising their voices in encouragement, they set their hands to the task, and at that moment they put Gorgias and his troops to flight.
Judas took his troops to a city called Sodom. As the Sabbath was approaching, they purified and washed themselves according to their laws and observed the Sabbath.

The next day they went through the region of Judea to gather the bodies of those who had fallen in battle, so that, together with their relatives, they might bury them in their respective tombs beside their ancestors.

When they reached the battlefield, they found the bodies of their brothers. Beneath their clothing they had amulet beads and charms from all sorts of idols, attached to their shoulder straps. The law especially abhorred these things and strictly forbade the Hebrews to engage in such practices. When they found this, they became convinced that these men had been killed for that reason.
Then all together they blessed the Lord, the righteous judge, who brings hidden secrets to light.

They bowed down and earnestly prayed that the sin which had been committed might be forgiven them. Brave Judas also encouraged the troops and urged them to guard against that same sin. He said, “You see with your own eyes the punishment that has come because of the sins committed.”

With courageous resolve, he collected four staters twice over and sent them to Jerusalem to offer sacrifices for sin. He acted with very sound wisdom, for in doing this he had the resurrection of the dead in mind.
For if he had no hope of the resurrection of those who had fallen in battle, offering prayers for the dead would have been vain and pointless.
But he looked to the gracious rewards kept in store for those who had died in righteousness.
With valor and courage, he considered making provision for the dead so that their sins might be forgiven.
In the one hundred and forty-ninth year, during the time of Judas, Antiochus came with many troops.

Together with Lysias, he came into Judea with one hundred and ten thousand shield-bearing soldiers, a force of five thousand three hundred cavalry, twenty-two elephants, and three hundred scythed chariots.
Simon had also joined them under a deceitful guise, as though he were pleading for peace in the land, while in his heart he coveted the high priesthood of the land.

But the King of kings greatly stirred Antiochus’s angry indignation against the lawless Simon. Lysias in particular also pointed out that this man was the cause of all the evils occurring in that land, and Antiochus ordered him seized and put to death on the spot according to the law.
There was a tower in that place, built fifty cubits high, filled with ashes and made round on every side.

Its door was built at a slant on the inside, leading into the ashes, at [?]. Into it they would throw anyone who had harmed the temple or was guilty of other very great crimes, by common agreement, making it turn with a mere touch of the hand.
They ordered that the lawless Simon be removed from their midst by such a death,

so that he would deserve neither burial in the earth nor a shroud in the land where he lived. For he had committed many evils against the altar where the sacred fire and ashes were. Therefore he ended his life by a death of suffocation in ashes.
King Antiochus, becoming still more savage in his intentions, came prepared to inflict crueler torments on the Hebrews than those inflicted under his father.
When Judas learned this, he instructed the people to cry out to the Lord night and day, so that, as on other occasions, he would now also help those
whom they wished to exclude from the laws of their fathers and from the holy temple, and would not consent to hand them over to the lawless Gentiles.
When they all stood united in this pledge, falling down and rolling on the ground with tears and fasting for three days without interruption, Judas encouraged them to be vigilant.
He himself took the elders of the people aside and entered into counsel with them. “Let us fortify these cities,” he said, “before the king’s troops enter Judea.

And let us go out courageously, by God’s will, to fight to the death for the laws, the city and the temple, the country and its sovereignty.” When he said this, they quickly took up a strong position in the region of the city of Modein with their troops. He pitched camp,

distributed the password, and entrusted himself, his troops, and the victory of his force to God. He took Aristides, a specially chosen young man, fully armed, and entered the king’s camp at night. With swords he slaughtered the night watchmen guarding the gates, about four thousand men, and killed the foremost elephant together with its driver on the spot. Having thus laid the gatekeepers low, he turned back.
At that time he filled the entire camp with confusion and trembling.
They all reached that morning dispirited, weakened, exhausted, and bewildered.
The king, having received such a taste of the bold courage of the Hebrew force through help from heaven, tried another stratagem and set out toward [?].
He raided Beth-zur and subjected it to a blockade, siegeworks, and a siege. Yet there too, after attacking and fighting, he was defeated.
For Judas himself supplied those inside with arrows, weapons, and provisions, bringing them in by concealed routes.
A man named Rhodocus from the Jewish force betrayed these plans and informed the enemy. He was investigated, sought out, found, punished, and put to death by the sword.

When the king’s violence became a warning to the fortified towns, he began to abandon force and work by deceit. He made agreements with those in the fortified towns and proceeded to take possession of the strongholds.

From there he attacked the Jews’ territory, but, defeated on both sides, he found himself in a sorry state. Then he received news of Philip’s furious advance: Philip had forcibly seized control of royal affairs and was moving through the country. He grew weak, lost heart, and became distressed. He appealed to the Hebrews and agreed with them, made a covenant, and swore to restore all their rights. He established peace and reconciliation between them, offered a sacrifice, and honored the temple. With compassion, love, and kindness, he treated them benevolently in all their settlements.
He honored Maccabeus and placed him over them with even greater dignity than before. He left Hegemonides there as commander over the country from Dor to Gerar.

He himself went into Ptolemais. The citizens were very angry about the peace agreement. They would not quiet down but persisted in their agitation, demanding that he revoke the agreement of reconciliation.

Lysias himself came forward and stood before them. He wisely won them over and calmed their minds. He then returned to the region of Antioch. This was how the king’s plundering expedition came to an end.
After an interval of three years, Demetrius of the Seleucids advanced against the Hebrews, entering through the harbor of Tripolis with a large contingent and many troops.
To march into the interior of the country and drive out Antiochus and his brother Lysias.

There was a certain man named Alcimus who had formerly been high priest. He had willingly defiled himself earlier, during the upheaval of the times. He thought to himself and said that, whatever the situation, it was impossible for him to find deliverance, and he could no longer approach the holy altar.

He came and stood before King Demetrius in the one hundred and fifty-first year, presenting him with golden crowns, palm branches, and leafy boughs in honor of the temple. That day he remained silent,

but he waited for an opportunity to find support for his folly. When one day Demetrius happened to summon him to a council, the king began questioning him: “What laws, wishes, and intentions do these Hebrews in Judea hold concerning us?”

He answered as follows: “Those among the Jews who are called Hasideans, whose commander and general is Judas Maccabeus, have risen up and gathered troops. They are prepared for battle, constantly stir up their assemblies, and do not allow them to submit peacefully to your rule.
“For this reason I have left behind my ancestral honor, the priesthood, and have come to you,

“first to show my heartfelt concern for royal affairs, and then for our own affairs. For I have come to you deeply troubled and anxious because of these men’s folly, since our entire nation is caught in unrest through no fault of its own.
“But I have learned and know all the peaceful intentions and benevolent wishes you have for every region and every country.
“Yet as long as Judas is alive, it is impossible for royal affairs in Judea to enjoy peace.”
When he began speaking this way about Judas, the other leading men, who bore grudges against Judas out of hostility, gathered around and further inflamed the king’s anger.

Then he immediately ordered Nicanor, the commander of the elephants, to be summoned. He put troops under his command, appointed him commander of the regions of Judea, and sent him off with extensive equipment.
With many instructions to seize Judas himself outright by force, scatter the entire company in every direction, and install Alcimus there as high priest of the great temple in Judea.
People of the nations who had fled from there because of Judas came in scattered groups and joined Nicanor’s army. They regarded the Jews’ misfortune as their own glory.

When they heard of Nicanor’s advance and such great agitation among the Gentiles, they put earth on their heads and prostrated themselves before the one who had established his people from the beginning of time and had always visibly come to the aid of his own allotted people.
When the commander gave the order, he quickly went out to meet him at a village named Dessau.
Simon, Judas’s brother, confronted Nicanor, but suffered a brief defeat because of his fellow soldiers’ lack of vigilance.
But Nicanor had heard of the men’s bravery and of the courageous struggle they had waged in battle for their country, and he was afraid to settle the dispute by bloodshed.
For this reason he sent for Posidonius, Theodotus, and Mattathias to negotiate and conclude an agreement.
After much uncertainty and discussion among them, the commander shared his proposal with many others, and the troops unanimously agreed to accept peace.

They proposed an agreement and made a treaty. They appointed a day on which they would meet in one place and confirm the agreement. They came together, set out seats, held a consultation, and made a treaty.

Judas ordered his own company to arm themselves, prepare, and take up positions in ambush, lest their enemies attempt some wicked treachery against them. Thus, with due caution, they established a proper agreement with one another.
Nicanor entered Jerusalem and went about without any disorderly or unlawful conduct. He dismissed the troops he had gathered, sending them back to their respective places.
Nicanor treated Judas with tenderness, gentleness, and easy affection.
He urged him to take a wife, so that affection might arise and he might have children. Judas accepted, agreed, made the arrangement, and established a household.

When Alcimus saw their mutual harmony and the agreement they had concluded, he hurried to Demetrius and accused Nicanor. He declared that Nicanor held contrary and disloyal intentions against the king’s commands, since he had adopted a man harmful to the king’s affairs and appointed him as his own heir and successor.

When the king heard the words of the lawless slanderer, he flew into a rage. The king ordered letters to be issued announcing that he did not approve of the agreement. In the same letter he commanded that Maccabeus be brought to the city of Antioch with his feet and hands bound.

When Nicanor was informed of all this, he was downcast and distraught, grieving inwardly that deceit might enter their agreement and that their pledges might be broken without cause, to the harm of an innocent man.
But because he could not disregard the king’s command, he sought an opportunity to carry it out.

When Maccabeus saw Nicanor approaching him more furiously and treating him with harsher and more boorish domination, he took Nicanor’s insolence badly. There, in Nicanor’s presence, he threw many people into confusion, and he himself departed from before Nicanor.

When Nicanor saw that he could not get the man into his hands as he wished, he went to the priests in the holy temple while they were offering sacrifices and sternly ordered them to hand the man over immediately.
They affirmed under oath, “We have not even seen that man.” He stretched out his hand toward the temple.

He swore as follows: “If you do not hand Judas over to me bound hand and foot, I will level this temple of God to the ground, overthrow this altar, and establish this temple as a sanctuary dedicated to the gods of Ormizd.”
After saying this, he departed. The priests raised their hands to heaven and called upon the one who had always been their nation’s helper and protector, saying:
“You, Lord of all, need nothing and are full of everything. It was your will to establish the temple of your dwelling among us.
And now, Lord, in all holiness, preserve forever this temple of yours, newly sanctified.”

There was a man named Razis, one of the elders of the people, from the forces of Jerusalem. He was very devoted to his companions and generous toward others, distinguished and highly respected, and because of his caring disposition he was called the father of the Hebrews.
For in former times he had served as a lawgiver for the pure and unadulterated laws of Judaism, and had devoted himself, body and soul, to complete freedom.
When Nicanor wished to display openly the hostility he bore toward the Jews, he assigned more than five hundred soldiers to go and seize them.
For he said, “These too will be put to shame and turn back, and I will accomplish a great deed against this city.”
When the troops arrived, they surrounded the tower and pressed hard against the door. They called to one another to bring fire so that they could burn the door.

When the man found himself in such distress and confusion, he gathered his thoughts, took command of himself, and thrust a sword below his navel. He wanted to die as a free man rather than fall into the hands of lawless men and defile his own nobility.
And with the sword he went straight inside because of the urgency of the danger. As the soldiers rushed through the doors, he wanted to climb up and throw himself down from a height over the wall.
When they rushed about here and there in confusion and the crowd scattered away from him, he put down the sword and went off on his own.

He stood there while his strength and spirit still remained. He came into view, fiercely filled with anger, even though his blood was flowing out in clots and his wounds were badly torn. The crowd before him scattered to either side.

He went up and stood on a rock facing both sides, bent down, gathered his intestines into his arms together with the blood, and held them up toward heaven. He called upon the Lord of life, of souls and bodies, and said, “Give him this same recompense.” And in this manner he departed from the world.
When Nicanor was informed about the Jews in the region of the Samaritans, he made plans and prepared to attack them on the Sabbath, the day of rest.

The Jews who were with him, whom Nicanor was taking along under compulsion, began to plead with him and say, “Far be it from you, lord! Do not carry out your wishes so harshly and savagely. Instead, give glory and honor to the day that the holy Almighty has honored as a day of rest.”
Then the lawless man began to question them, saying, “Is there an almighty God in heaven who commanded you to keep the Sabbath day at ease?”
They answered and said, “Yes, there is a living, all-powerful Lord who commanded us to keep the seventh day, the Sabbath, at ease.”

The vicious man said contemptuously, “The mighty ruler of this earth is the one who commands the use of weapons and equipment and the performance of royal duties.” Yet the lawless man did not relent in his arrogance.
Nicanor proceeded with complete arrogance and stubbornness, expecting to overtake the Jews, destroy them, and erect a monument of victory.
But Maccabeus always trusted in the Lord, who never withheld his help from him.

He encouraged those who were with him not to grow weary or hesitate to attack the lawless Gentiles, but to keep in mind their former deeds of courage and the help they had received from heaven, and now to expect the same victory and encouragement from the Lord.
He encouraged them from the Law and the Prophets, reminding them of the battles that had been fought by their hands.
He strengthened their hearts and made them still more willing by also bringing up the Gentiles’ falsehoods, their breaking of covenants, and their disregard for oaths.
He fired up each of them more with encouraging words than with weapons, spears, and shields. He also began to tell them a dream suited to the occasion, which made them all still more cheerful.

The vision in the dream was like this: a certain Onias, who had formerly been high priest, handsome in appearance and splendid to behold, gentle in character and calm in heart, came forward and spoke graciously, as had been his habit from childhood in all the excellence of his character. Raising his hands, he prayed for the stability of the Hebrew people.
Then he saw an old man of wondrous glory, surrounded by something exceedingly beautiful.
Then Onias began to speak and said, “Brother, this old man is the one who continually offers many prayers to God without ceasing: Jeremiah, the prophet of God.”
Jeremiah stretched out his right hand and placed in Judas’s hand a sword adorned with gold. As he gave it, he said:
“Take this sword, a holy gift from the Lord, so that with it you may destroy all your enemies.”

They were encouraged by Judas’s powerful and beautiful words, and their courage rose greatly. The young men’s spirits were renewed. From then on they resolved not to waver this way and that, but to plant their feet firmly, rely on endurance, stand strong in battle, win a name for courage, uphold the terms of the covenant of equality, and undertake the struggle for the city,

for their wives and children and their own brothers, for their nurses, homes, and fellow citizens of their own clans. More than all these, their struggle in battle was for the great, sanctified temple.
Among the citizens within the city, too, the distress over the battle and the expectation of a painful judgment were no small matter.

As the divisions of the two armies approached one another, the trumpet sounded, preparations were made, and the battle line was drawn up. They positioned the armored elephants at the head of the troops, division by division, and formed the cavalry into right and left wings.

Judas looked upon that terrifying sight: the troops drawn up under their various banners, the gleaming of the different weapons, the fluttering standards, and the overwhelming ferocity of the enormous beasts. Raising his hands to heaven, he called upon the wonder-working Lord, who grants victory to those worthy of him, not according to human wishes but according to his own just will.

He began his supplication in these words: “You, Lord of lords, sent your angel in the days of King Hezekiah, and you destroyed one hundred and eighty-five thousand fully armed horsemen from Sennacherib’s army.

“And now, almighty Lord, who dwell in heaven, send your angel before us, bringing terror, fear, and trembling through the strength of your arm, so that they may be struck with terror and become powerless—
“those who have come against your people with blasphemy.” And he finished speaking.
Meanwhile, Nicanor advanced his battle line with great pomp, to the blare of the trumpet and the sound of many instruments.
But those on this side charged against them with many prayers and supplications,

putting their hands to the task and directing their hearts toward God in heaven through prayer. Judas’s Maccabean troops advanced and struck down no fewer than thirty-five thousand of the pagan army, rejoicing greatly at the manifest help of God’s mighty power.

Having thus completed their joyful undertaking, they returned with gladness. There they found Nicanor fallen before the slaughtered troops, with his weapons, ornaments, and insignia, between the two battle lines.
With loud cries and a great shout, they blessed almighty God in their ancestral language.

The man who had fought for the nation with strength and steadfastness, with united courage and valor and wholehearted resolve, gave orders. He commanded that Nicanor’s head and his right hand, together with the shoulder, be cut off and taken to Jerusalem.
When he himself arrived, he summoned the members of his nation and the priests before the altar, and had the guards of the citadel, the Akra, brought there.
He showed them the head of the lawless, blasphemous Nicanor and the hand that he had dared to stretch out against the temple of almighty God with arrogant boasting.

He commanded that the tongue of the lawless Nicanor be cut out and said, “I will cut this into tiny pieces and feed it to the birds as carrion.” He also ordered that the arm of that senseless man be hung up facing the temple.
But everyone blessed the God who had appeared from heaven, saying, “Blessed is he who has kept his holy place undefiled!”
And he hung Nicanor’s head from the fortified tower, plainly visible to everyone, and it stood as a sign of victory, clearly showing the Lord’s help.
Together they made a pledge and, with the unanimous consent of the whole nation, decreed that this day should be observed as an annual feast, so that they would not let the day pass unmarked.
The date appointed was the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, called Adar in the Syrian language, which was one day before the month of Mordecai.
That is all there is to say about the events concerning Nicanor. And since the Hebrews gained possession of the city from that time onward, I too will end my account at this point.
And if these things are well arranged, may I be praised for arranging them here; this is what I too desire. But if the account is plain and weak, this was all I could do.

For just as drinking wine alone, or water alone, is unappealing, but mixing water with wine makes its flavor sweet and pleasant, so the arrangement of an account delights the ears of those who hear it. Let this be the end of my account. The Second Book of Maccabees is completed.
